episode_title: Private Equity: The Curious and Incurious

real_qa.q: What are the distinctive factors that separate a great private equity organization from a poor one in the lumber and building materials industry?
real_qa.r: Private equity itself is not bad—there are some great actors, average actors, and poor actors. The key differentiators are arrogance, strategy, and purpose. Those who enter without industry knowledge or treat it as a pure money play without understanding the business give private equity a bad name. In contrast, successful private equity groups bring strategic vision, invest in people and career paths, create strong operating platforms, and have a long-term buy-and-hold strategy rather than just seeking a five to seven-year exit.
real_qa.requete: good vs bad private equity lumber industry

real_qa.q: Why did post-COVID private equity investments in lumber and building materials often fail compared to pre-Great Recession and post-Great Recession periods?
real_qa.r: Pre-Great Recession, private equity was strategic and selective with buy-and-hold strategies. After 2008, talented industry operators started their own ventures backed by PE. However, COVID made lumber look like easy money—shooting fish in a barrel. This attracted investors with no strategy, no industry understanding, and no long-term commitment, only seeking five to seven-year exits. Rising housing demand created false security, making even poor operators appear successful, and many new entrants lacked the operating platform and strategy needed to navigate commodity volatility and housing start dynamics.
real_qa.requete: why private equity lumber failed after COVID
